project.name: kalend

tour.title: Project Guide & Architecture
tour.description: CLAUDE.md is the authoritative guide to Kalend's architecture, conventions, and development workflow. It documents the full directory layout, the authentication pattern, the API layer pattern, and the rendering strategy — making it the ideal starting point before exploring any code. Reading this first gives you a mental map that connects every subsequent file in the tour.

tour.title: App Layout & Entry Point
tour.description: app/layout.tsx is the root Next.js layout that sets global HTML metadata, loads fonts, and mounts the global React context providers via Providers.tsx. app/page.tsx is the public-facing landing page that surfaces the platform's calendar features, tools, and public API — it is the first page a visitor sees and shows which capabilities the product exposes. Together these two files frame the entire frontend shell.
tour.languageLesson: In Next.js 14 App Router, layout.tsx wraps every child route in its segment. The root layout is the single place to add global providers, fonts, and <html>/<body> tags — child layouts layer on top without re-rendering the root.

tour.title: Edge Middleware & Auth
tour.description: middleware.ts runs on every incoming request at the edge before any page or API handler is reached. It uses the Supabase server client to read the session cookie and enforces role-based access control: /admin/* requires an admin role, /dashboard/* requires an authenticated user, and public routes pass through unmodified. This file is the security boundary for the entire application.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js edge middleware executes in the V8 edge runtime (not Node.js), so only Web APIs and edge-compatible packages are available. The matcher config in middleware.ts limits which paths trigger the middleware, avoiding unnecessary overhead on static assets.

tour.title: Data Schema & Database Models
tour.description: prisma/schema.prisma defines the seven core database models: Country, Region, Holiday, Profile, UserEvent, ApiKey, and ApiUsageLog. These models are the canonical source of truth for all data shapes in the application — every service in lib/ and every API route in app/api/ ultimately reads or writes these tables. Understanding the schema before exploring the service layer reveals why each piece of business logic is structured the way it is.
tour.languageLesson: Prisma schema uses a declarative syntax where each model maps to a database table. Relations are expressed as typed fields (e.g., Holiday[] on Country) and Prisma generates fully-typed query methods from them, eliminating hand-written SQL for standard CRUD operations.

tour.title: Prisma Client Singleton
tour.description: lib/prisma.ts exports a singleton PrismaClient instance that is reused across all server-side modules. In Next.js development mode the module hot-reloads frequently, and without a singleton pattern each reload would open a new database connection pool, exhausting PostgreSQL connections quickly. The singleton is the foundation that every data-fetching function in lib/calendar/ and the API routes depends on.
tour.languageLesson: The standard Next.js pattern attaches the PrismaClient to the Node.js global object in development (global.prisma) so that module hot-reloading reuses the existing instance. In production, the module is loaded once and the global trick is skipped.

tour.title: Calendar Constants & Domain Vocabulary
tour.description: lib/calendar/constants.ts defines the shared vocabulary for the entire calendar domain: Indonesian month and day names, the full country list, Chinese zodiac (shio) cycle, Hijri year mappings, and the supported year range. Every other calendar module imports from here, making this file the single source of truth for display values and domain boundaries. Reviewing it reveals the breadth of calendar systems the platform supports.

tour.title: Core Holiday Data Service
tour.description: lib/calendar/holidays.ts is the most widely depended-upon file in the codebase (fan-in 4) — it is imported by the public year page, month page, the DayCell component, and the v1 API route. It fetches Indonesian public holidays from PostgreSQL via the Prisma client from Step 5, applies in-memory caching to avoid redundant database queries, and exports focused query utilities for filtering by year, month, or date. This is the heart of the calendar data pipeline.
tour.languageLesson: In-memory caching at the module level persists for the lifetime of a serverless function instance. For Next.js on Vercel this means cache hits are common within a warm instance but the cache is cold-started on each new deployment or cold invocation — a trade-off between simplicity and predictability.

tour.title: Javanese & Long Weekend Calculators
tour.description: lib/calendar/weton.ts implements the Javanese weton calendar system, converting any Gregorian date into its pasaran cycle day, neptu score, and combined weton name — cultural data displayed on the day detail page. lib/calendar/longweekend.ts builds on the holidays service to detect long weekends and compute optimal leave (cuti) strategies, powering the cuti optimizer tool. Both libraries are pure computation modules with no side effects, making them straightforward to unit-test.
tour.languageLesson: Pure functions with deterministic outputs are ideal candidates for unit testing. The weton logic has its own weton.test.ts sibling file using Vitest — the tests run in milliseconds because there is no database or network dependency.

tour.title: Public Calendar Pages
tour.description: The three nested dynamic routes — app/(public)/[year]/page.tsx, app/(public)/[year]/[month]/page.tsx, and app/(public)/[year]/[month]/[date]/page.tsx — form the core public UI of Kalend. Each page server-renders its data by calling the holidays library directly, with the year page showing an annual overview, the month page showing a filterable list, and the day page adding weton details and user events. The nesting follows the natural hierarchy of time.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js App Router uses folder-based dynamic segments ([year], [month], [date]) that nest cleanly. Each segment's page.tsx receives params as a prop. Because these are React Server Components, the database fetch happens on the server — no client-side loading state, no API call from the browser.

tour.title: Calendar UI Components
tour.description: components/calendar/MonthGrid.tsx renders the interactive month view by composing a grid of DayCell components, one per calendar day. components/calendar/DayCell.tsx is where the visual logic lives: it highlights holidays, shows the weton label from Step 8, and marks days with user events. DayCell imports both the holidays library and the weton library, making it the component that brings the domain data together into a visible, interactive cell.
tour.languageLesson: This is the classic container/presentational component split. MonthGrid owns layout and iteration logic, while DayCell owns the per-day display logic. Keeping them separate makes it easy to swap the grid layout without rewriting cell rendering, or to reuse DayCell in other contexts like a weekly view.

tour.title: Authentication Pages
tour.description: app/(auth)/login/page.tsx is the auth entry point, supporting both email/password login and Google OAuth via Supabase. The (auth) route group shares a layout that is separate from the public and dashboard layouts, providing a clean focused UI for unauthenticated flows. After a successful login, the middleware from Step 3 handles the session cookie and redirects users to their intended destination.

tour.title: User Dashboard
tour.description: app/(dashboard)/dashboard/page.tsx is the authenticated home page, aggregating a user's personal event summary alongside upcoming public holidays. It sits inside the (dashboard) route group which middleware guards — only authenticated sessions reach this page. This page demonstrates the pattern of combining personal user data (from the Profile and UserEvent models in the schema) with the shared holiday dataset.

tour.title: Public REST API
tour.description: app/api/v1/holidays/route.ts is the public-facing REST endpoint for holiday data, accepting year, month, or date query parameters. It wraps its handler with the withApiAuth HOF from lib/api/middleware.ts, which validates the Bearer API key, enforces per-key rate limits, and logs each request to ApiUsageLog — the same Prisma model defined in Step 4. The OpenAPI spec in content/docs/openapi.yaml documents the full v1 contract for API consumers.
tour.languageLesson: The Higher-Order Function (HOF) pattern for API middleware — withApiAuth wraps any handler function and returns a new function — is idiomatic TypeScript for cross-cutting concerns. It keeps auth/rate-limit logic out of individual route files and makes each concern independently testable.

tour.title: Admin Panel
tour.description: app/admin/holidays/page.tsx is the admin interface for managing the holiday dataset that powers the entire platform. It is protected at the middleware layer (requires admin role) and provides search, filtering, and CRUD operations over the Holiday table defined in the Prisma schema. The admin panel is how the authoritative holiday data enters the system before being served to public visitors and API consumers.

tour.title: Email & Deployment
tour.description: lib/email/index.ts implements transactional emails via the Resend service, sending welcome messages, API key delivery, and event reminder notifications — the last of which is triggered by a cron job. vercel.json configures those cron schedules on Vercel, running the reminder job and a keep-alive ping on fixed intervals. Together these two files close the loop on the platform's automated operations.
tour.languageLesson: Vercel cron jobs defined in vercel.json send GET requests to an API route on the configured schedule. The cron route must be protected (e.g., by a secret header) to prevent public invocation, and must complete within Vercel's function timeout — long jobs should be offloaded to a background queue.
